candidate.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity → Reduction of Risk Potential: recognize complications of diagnostic or therapeutic procedures, perform focused assessment, monitor for changes in client condition, and intervene/escalate when a complication is suspected.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Recognition of procedure-related complications and focused reassessment
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize new confusion and asterixis after TIPS as possible post-TIPS hepatic encephalopathy requiring prompt focused assessment and escalation rather than assuming a benign postprocedure effect or shunt occlusion.

options.A: These findings are concerning for post-TIPS hepatic encephalopathy and require prompt focused assessment and communication with the treating team.
options.B: These findings are an expected harmless effect of portal decompression and do not require evaluation unless they persist for several weeks.
options.C: These findings prove that the TIPS is occluded because hepatic encephalopathy occurs only when portal decompression has failed.
options.D: These findings are best explained by routine venous-access discomfort and are unrelated to the physiologic effects of portosystemic shunting.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. AASLD identifies hepatic encephalopathy as a well-known and clinically important complication after TIPS. TIPS redirects portal blood into the systemic circulation and reduces first-pass hepatic clearance of neurotoxins, so new disorientation and asterixis after the procedure are compatible with hepatic encephalopathy and warrant prompt assessment rather than reassurance. Current NCBI guidance also identifies TIPS and other portosystemic shunts as causes of hepatic encephalopathy and lists confusion, disorientation, altered attention, and asterixis among clinically relevant findings. B is incorrect because new neurologic changes are not a harmless expected finding to ignore. C is incorrect because hepatic encephalopathy can occur with a functioning TIPS and does not by itself prove shunt occlusion. D is incorrect because venous-access discomfort does not explain a new encephalopathic mental-status change and asterixis. The final item narrows the construct to one high-value post-TIPS complication instead of bundling encephalopathy, access-site bleeding, and shunt-patency surveillance into a single recall answer.
candidate.source_claim_supported: AASLD and NCBI directly support hepatic encephalopathy as a major post-TIPS complication caused in part by portosystemic diversion and reduced hepatic clearance; new disorientation and asterixis are compatible with hepatic encephalopathy and require clinical evaluation.
